meta_title: Connect to VpnHood! SERVER Through a Domain Name | VpnHood!
meta_description: Give VpnHood! SERVER a domain name with a trusted certificate, on a managed server or a standalone one, so its keys find the server through DNS.
title: Connect through a domain name
lead: Out of the box, the server presents a self-signed certificate with a made-up name, and its access keys lead to its IP address. Give it a domain name you own, with a certificate from a certificate authority, and a connection to it looks like a visit to an ordinary website.
why_keys: Keys made after the change carry the domain. Apps look it up when they connect and check the server's certificate the way a browser does, so if you move the server to a new IP address, you point the domain at it and those keys keep working.
why_ips: The keys still carry the server's IP addresses too, so an app that cannot look the domain up connects as before.
req_domain: A domain or a subdomain you control, such as [domain_example]. Use a single name, not a wildcard.
req_dns: A DNS record that points it at the server's connection IP: an A record, and an AAAA record if the server has an IPv6 address. Point it straight at the server, not through a CDN's proxy.
req_port: On a managed server, TCP port [port_http] open, for as long as you use the domain: the certificate is checked through it, and renewed through it every few months.
mgr_add: In VpnHood! MANAGER, open [manager_server_farms] and then the farm. Under [manager_certificates], select [manager_add], enter the domain as [manager_domain_name] and select [manager_create]. MANAGER creates a self-signed certificate for it and opens it.
mgr_autosign: Edit [manager_signing] and choose [manager_autosign]. MANAGER asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate, which checks the domain through your server on TCP port [port_http]. When it is done, [manager_signature] reads [manager_ca_signed], and MANAGER renews the certificate by itself before it expires.
mgr_token: Then edit [manager_visibility] and choose [manager_public_in_token]. Every key of the farm now carries the domain, and the farm's previous certificate becomes [manager_public].
mgr_keys: Keys you copy from MANAGER from now on carry the domain. Apps holding an older key get the new one when they connect, as [manager_push_token] is on by default. Keep the farm's previous certificate until then: older keys work only while it is there.
mgr_failed: If the check fails, [manager_signing] shows why, and after a few failed attempts it goes back to [manager_manual]. Fix the DNS record or open the port, then choose [manager_autosign] again.
mgr_check: To check, open the farm: under [manager_access_points], the domain comes first.
mgr_server_level: A server's own page has a [manager_certificates] list too. A certificate there belongs to that one server, so add the domain your keys carry to the farm instead.
file_cert: A standalone server cannot get a certificate by itself. Get one for the domain from a certificate authority, as a PFX file with its private key, and put it in place of [server_cert_pfx], under the same name.
file_settings: Then put the file's password in [setting_ssl_password] and set [setting_is_valid_host_name] to [json_true], both under [setting_file_access_manager] in [server_appsettings]. A new install has no such file: create it, and from then on the server uses it in place of the settings it was installed with.
caption_file: The whole file, with your certificate's password in place of the example
file_name: The server takes the domain from the certificate itself, so there is no setting for it.
file_restart: Restart the server with [server_restart_linux], or with [docker_restart] in Docker. With a wrong password it does not start, and its log says [log_could_not_start]
file_keys: Keys made before the change stop working, as they expect the old certificate. Print each of them again and give your users the new key: its options and its usage stay the same. A key's ID is the name of its file in [server_access_dir], without [key_file_ext].
caption_print: List the keys, then print one again by its ID
file_docker: In Docker, run the same through [docker_exec_supervisor], as for [vhserver_gen].
file_renew: The new keys carry the domain and no longer depend on the certificate itself, so they keep working when you renew it: put the new file in place and restart the server.
